title: SYSK Distraction Playlist: How Jim Henson Worked
summary: A distraction-playlist episode (a rerun-style companion to the Muppets episode) about Jim Henson's life and career. The hosts open with banter about sensitivity-training videos and Henson's reputation as a genuinely good, hard-working man, then trace his early years in Mississippi and at college, his experimental films (including The Cube and Time Piece), his commercial puppetry company and Rolf and Cookie Monster origins, Sesame Street, Kermit's development, the Muppet Show, Fraggle Rock, Muppet Babies, the Muppet Movie, The Dark Crystal, Labyrinth, The Jim Henson Hour and Storyteller, his death from a strep infection, and the later sale and ownership of the Muppets and Sesame Street characters. A listener mail segment on the Dark Ages and Islamic world closes the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and sensitivity training
segments.summary: The hosts open with jokes about sensitivity-training videos and say Jim Henson was genuinely a good person, not a figure with a hidden dark side. Frank Oz's remarks about Henson are discussed.

segments.title: Henson's early life, college, and experimental films
segments.summary: Henson was born in 1936 in Mississippi and was inspired by his maternal grandmother. He studied at college in Maryland, graduating with a home economics degree because it was the only one offering puppet-making courses. He made experimental films, including Time Piece, which earned an Academy Award nomination, and The Cube, a 1969 NBC experimental TV piece.

segments.title: Early commercials and the first Muppets
segments.summary: After a European tour, Henson decided to pursue puppetry and formed a commercial company in New York in 1963, hiring Frank Oz and Jerry Juhl. He retained rights to his creations, so characters such as Cookie Monster, first made for a chip ad, and Rolf, from Purina commercials and The Jimmy Dean Show, came to be Muppets.

segments.title: Sesame Street and puppets on television
segments.summary: Henson joined the Children's Television Workshop for Sesame Street in 1969 and created most of its iconic characters without being its creator. He directed some of the short films. Television allowed puppets new camera-based possibilities. Platforming let performers stand, and foam materials gave puppets expressive faces suited to close-ups.

segments.title: Center for Puppetry Arts and puppetry community
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Center for Puppetry Arts in Atlanta, which received about five hundred puppets from Henson, and local Atlanta puppeteers they know.

segments.title: The Muppet Show, Saturday Night Live, and Fraggle Rock
segments.summary: Henson's SNL work in season one was not a major success. His break came when Lew Grade in London gave him a deal, producing The Muppet Show, a backstage variety show. Rubber Ducky reached number sixteen on the Billboard chart in 1970. Fraggle Rock, one of HBO's first original series, followed.

segments.title: Muppet Babies and Ron Funches aside
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Muppet Babies, a cartoon they watched at different points in its run, and mention comedian Ron Funches's bit about the show.

segments.title: Movies, Dark Crystal, Labyrinth, and later TV
segments.summary: Henson's other work included Ripples and Wheels with Raymond Scott, the Floating Face sketch, The Muppet Movie, The Dark Crystal (1982, co-directed with Frank Oz, based on Brian Froud's drawings, initially weak at the box office), and Labyrinth, written by Terry Jones and featuring David Bowie. Later TV included The Jim Henson Hour and The Storyteller, which featured the film-noir Dog City narrated by Rolf, with Kevin Clash as Ah Sue.

segments.title: Henson's death, legacy, and sale of the Muppets
segments.summary: Henson died in 1990 of organ failure caused by a strep infection. Jane Henson founded the Jim Henson Legacy. Henson had planned a sale to Disney for $150 million, but his children sold the company in 2000 for $80 million, and it was bought back later. Disney now owns the Muppets, and the Creature Shop still builds Sesame Street puppets.

segments.title: Listener mail: the Dark Ages and the Islamic world
segments.summary: A listener named Matt, a high school sophomore, writes that the Dark Ages were not dark in the Islamic world, covering scholarship, algebra, and mosque construction. The hosts sign off with ways to send suggestions.
